title: How Ancient Societies Viewed Mental Illness and the Horrific Treatments of That Time
subtitle: When it comes to mental illness, we’ve come a long way since the days of superstition and sorcery. But we still have work to do.
author: Avery Hurt

annotations.comment: This one was a bit strange. The introduction and some other parts feel like they were written by a human, especially things like "drinking the blood of a gladiator"  and "electroconvulsive therapy without anaesthesia" which both seem pretty brutal. However, the introduction of Dr. Sarah Thompson and Dr. Emily Carter (who by now has more than a lifetime's worth of qualifications), means that it has to be AI text. The conclusion also seems very AI-generated as it's far too generic and hopeful.

There are several often-used AI words and phrases which I've highlighted. The concluding sentences are a typical AI summary of what was said before. There are several sentences containing lists, which is another AI signature.
Here's why I think it's AI. Sounds very business-like. Follows the same AI structure. No errors. Stiff. First quote usually starts with someone 'explaining' something. Textbook conclusion.

I am pretty confident this is AI-generated. While I struggled at first, what gave me an indicator was the format, or the outline. When AI generates a topic for a blog, it creates very generalized headers, often resorting to "Conclusion", "How does (topic) work" or "Understanding (topic)" or something similar. From there, I found that many of the sentences included those flowery summarizing sections, such as "a greater emphasis on empathy and compassion", and "a shift towards a more naturalistic understanding of mental health". The conclusion sentences solidified my choice for me, but I also feel that this article contains some human edits for variety in sentence structure and AI checker bypassing. So, it's AI-generated.

AI wordiness is becoming more obvious the more of these texts I read. AI should be trained to vary the way it introduces people: a this or a that gets pretty tedious after a while. Did AI pick up the use of "individual(s)" for person and people from us (humans) or is the increased use of this abomination an influence of AI on human language?
